title: A deep dive down the network stack
topic: HTTP and the layers below it
note: A developer's questions in one session, from the top of the HTTP stack down to the link layer. The set is pinned so that a later run changes only the prose, never the questions. This follows the rule the corpus manifest states: hold the content still, and the form is the only thing left to measure.
provenance: Written by an agent that never read the standard, under a rule that forbade it from naming writing, style or clarity. A question that asks for plain prose would prompt the register this eval measures.
questions: how does http actually work when i type a url into the browser and hit enter
you mentioned the client opens a connection before the request goes out — what's actually happening in that handshake, and why does it need a round trip before any data moves?
wait, why does that handshake need to happen again if I already talked to the same server five minutes ago? shouldn't it remember me?
ok but what's actually inside a TLS certificate, and what stops someone from just making their own and handing it to my browser?
walk me through the steps to capture and inspect the TCP handshake for a single request on my machine, start to finish
what happens below TLS — how does TCP know a packet got lost and make sure it's resent in order?
if i set the MTU too low on an interface, or mess with it on a router in the path, what actually breaks, and how would I even notice?
last one — at the link layer, what's the actual difference between a switch and a router, and how do they know where to send a frame vs a packet?
